title: Colston Loveland, Kalif Raymond, Gervon Dexter Sr. on start of veteran minicamp | Press Conference
text: Good to see you guys in a while. What's the >> evidence you're seeing at this part of the calendar that this offense is is moving toward a direction where it can be really explosive when when camp gets here? >> Um I think just I mean if we're comparing last year, you don't want to think about last year too much obviously, but um just more completions and you're seeing everyone's in the right spot. Um things are just flowing a little smoother. Obviously, you seen there's a lot to clean up still and a lot to get better at, which is exciting news cuz it's always a good thing when you have more to more to get and more to do. But, uh, yeah, I think things are going well. We got to finish these next two days off, right, though, >> how do you feel the continuity of of the the quarterback being the same, the play caller being the same, a lot of guys around you being the same. >> Uh, yeah, it's good. I mean, obviously in this league, you never know how it could be year to year. Um, so having familiar guys and guys who you can trust and know how they how they move, how they think, uh, I think that's important. Coin Benson, you're one of the most consistent players he's ever been around. What does being consistent mean to you? >> Uh, I'd say being consistent is coming in. You're going to have bad feel good, feel bad, have different days obviously. Um, but I think it's just not letting anyone know that and then continuing to do what you do and and Ben always says it, uh, just 1% better, be better than we were yesterday. And, uh, I think that's consistent in my book. I think not changing your routine, sticking to a routine that works for you. And uh like I said, there's going to be good and bad days. You're going to mess up. You're going to do better things on this day, but it's just staying levelheaded, not getting too high and too low. >> Ben talked about expanding your boundary a little bit now. Just knowing the comfort of where you are from where you were a year ago. Did you feel kind of the the confidence coming from that coaching staff and the way that they see what you can be for this offense? >> Yeah, for sure. Um you know, they I feel like they got a lot of trust in me, I got a lot of trust in them. They got a lot of trust in all the weapons we have. So, we know that they're going to put us in the best position to be successful and whatever they ask of all of us, we're going to go out there and do. >> With some of the individual sessions you and some of the receivers have been doing with Caleb, like what are your personal goals to get out of those sessions? >> Uh, I think one having fun. One, getting together, building that camaraderie. Um, offseason, you know, let's let's throw so throw some balls around, have some fun. Um, and then two, timing, rhythm, hitting, throwing the ball where it needs to be thrown and catching it, being in the right spot. Um, things we all talked about, and I think that definitely helps. >> One of those guys you've been with is uh is is Luther. You got obviously you guys came in together and you've been in some of these workouts with him. What have you seen from him? >> He's the truth, man. He's the truth. Nothing but the truth. Uh, the way he works, his attitude, his mindset. He's a guy you want on your team for sure. the chemistry with Caleb. Do you see any improvement in that chemistry, timing, rhythm, ball placement? >> Yeah, for sure. Um, most definitely. I think kind of what I said earlier, things are hitting at a faster and better rate than they were last year. Um, but still a lot on both ends, drops, miss throws, completion, that that'll boost the completion percentage. Um, and that's all of us collectively and we're aware of that and we know that, you know, we need to continue to grow in that aspect. the success you had as a rookie, like what did you take into the offseason thinking, okay, I want to take a step here. What did you specifically want to work on? >> Yeah, I think it's uh watching the tape and knowing like it was good. It was good for a rookie, but it's not going to be good enough for a second year or third year guy. So, knowing that all right, that flush that um like you said, clean up on the tape and that certain things I need to get better at, which is dang near everything. So, uh, but yeah, I think it's just going to the offseason knowing knowing what my strengths and flaws were definitely helps to see what I can focus on, especially coming in this six week, uh, window we had before camp. >> What's an example of that where you saw something on tape where you you reflect back and go, "Man, that just wasn't good enough." >> Uh, yeah. I think of um like for example in the run game, it's like a stalemate or just kind of hanging on, you know, and runners not getting touched or whatever. I'm doing my job. technically, but it's not good enough to put on tape. I think you need to put dominant um you know, and real good stuff on tape. Really dominating someone, moving someone. I think that's the next step. >> You were pretty open last offseason about being frustrated with the injury situation. How much uh how much benefit is that your mental just be able to be healthy right now and attacking everything full go? >> Yeah, it's great, man. All all glory to God uh for being healthy uh being out there with the teammates during OTAAS. This is fun. Um where else would you rather be? You said you were what you did last year was good for a rookie at over 700 yards receiving. So, you expect that number to go up, but like if you expect a thousand yards out of yourself? >> Uh, yeah. I think that's what you that's what I would like to say. But like I've always said, it's about what the team needs and what the coaching staff needs and what what whatever position I'm put in, I'm going to accept that role and attack that role um and do what I'm asked. And if that means going over 1,000, if it means going over under 400, you know, as long as we're winning games and getting the main goal and keeping the main thing the main thing. So, >> you think do you think the defensive coordinators spent their off season trying to game plan for you? >> Uh, I don't know, man. I think it's tough because we got so many weapons, you know, you can't just game plan around one guy. Um, then you'll get bit on the other side. So, >> a different situation than last year when maybe there was maybe the league didn't know what you were capable of, do you think? >> Uh, yeah. Yeah, sure. Maybe there might be a little more awareness now. Um, but like I said, I mean, there's a lot of dudes on the field who can make a play, so pick your poison. >> Thank you guys. >> Thank you. >> When Ben was in here earlier, he talked about how he expects you to be a big part of the offense. Just what are your thoughts on that and how has it been so far getting getting used to everything >> Uh, man, dude, I tell you, it's been wonderful here. Um, the transition uh to a new team is always it's a thing. I mean, even just from a rhythm routine. First, I remember the first day we just had an OTAAS. I was like, "Oh, snap. This is my first practice somewhere else in a long time. So, I don't even know where to go half the time. So, um just a lot of that stuff. But, uh I was telling everybody, man, this is a this right now is a time for foundation. Um it's kind of like pajamas right now. So, all the real stuff starts at training camp. So, we're building foundation so that way when we hit camp, you hit the wrong ground running." So, this is just part of a long process to be ready to come week one. So, >> how much of this is new to you? like different terminology or whatever Ben is doing now compared to what he was doing before. >> Um, some of the stuff I've heard before. Um, the differences here, there's a lot of things that are there's one thing here that's now changed versus where I'm coming from. So, um, some stuff's the same, some stuff's new. Um, so there is a bit of studying still still going on. Um, cuz you're in new spots and then hearing it, uh, like I said, a lot a good bit of it is different, too. So, that's a little bit of a change. >> Preferred destination because of, you know, you've worked with Ben before or how did it come together? >> I mean, I actually like listen when you under have you seen the way Ben works. Um, to be able to be near him, to work with him, work for him, all that stuff, man, it's a blessing. But especially in free agency, man, a lot of that stuff you don't really know what's coming. You know, you ask my agent like, "Hey, man, you know, I just I just want to play football." the rest of the stuff is kind of like you let it go. But to be here with him, um to have been with him is a blessing in all in all respects. So, um I was very excited and very thankful that I had opportunity to come and play with him and play for him. So, >> when you played for Ben, how did you see him try to kind of stay ahead of defensive coordinators uh as a play caller? >> Oh, man. Dude, >> that's the cool part. Uh is >> you don't you don't really know. I mean, he's got so much stuff going on and uh he'll blurt something out like, "Yeah, watch this. watch this the same play, watch this in two weeks. Like, so like he's not telling everybody this, but he'll just, you know, you just get a chance to talk to speak with him. He's like, I already know what this safety's going to do two weeks from now. And it's going to play don't work for this team, but in two weeks, watch what we do to this guy. And sure enough, you come in two weeks and it's like touchdown. Like, oh my. So, like just watching the way he processes things, uh, the cast that he has around him, he has the guys around him, the coaches around him for a reason because he knows what he's trying to do and, uh, his ideas, you know, he's very got an expansive mind. So, um, if sometimes he needs to be reelled back in, he's got guys in the room like, "Hey, you know what? We'll look at this aspect." So, I'm excited for it. >> The history with him and then being here for a couple months, can you tell that this is a team that's like built in his vision? >> Um, I think the guys that are here are the guys that they want to have here. Um, and it's not from the I don't know if I was about the performance stuff, but the daytoday stuff like Coloulston getting a 100 jugs before practice. I'm like, "Hey, you want to get some drugs?" Just like we got Xavian, me and Zavon just spent another 30 40 minutes after practice catching jugs. So like just you got guys with the work ethic, the will. Um, you got that those kind of guys in the building. So, >> that's like that's reflective of Ben. >> I think it's reflective of of Ben, Ryan, and where we're trying where they're trying to go the team, what they envision for this team. title: Ben Johnson: 'We have a slew of weapons we're looking to maximize' | Press Conference
text: good good uh week last week. I thought the guys uh continue to get better. They're working hard. Um we're very pleased with where they're at as a staff right now and uh this week will really be an extension of that. Uh good work on the grass and then some some meetings on the back end to to tie it all together. So uh good place right there. Of course, this time of year we're not no one's making the team. No one's really earning a roll quite yet. That'll all get figured out in training camp, but communication keeps improving and uh really pleased with with where guys are at right now. So, I'll open it up from there. When >> you got here, you said, "I'm not putting in the Lions offense. I'm putting in the Bears offense." Now that there's a year of that on tape, and defensive coordinators have had the offseason to study it. How do you balance doing what running the stuff that you run with making it look a little different or coming up with a twist that's that they might not be ready for in year two? >> Um, yeah, that's it's really I I feel like we're so multiple in what we do and and what we've put on tape. Um it's really not a huge concern of mine of of teams feeling like they got a beat on it. Um I think we got a quarterback like we have too. There's a lot of unpredictability that comes along with it. And so as he continues to grow and develop um you know if the structure of the play is there for him then he'll take it. But what he can do out of structure is is really unique and I think it makes us even more difficult to defend. So, um, our guys do a great job, our our coaching staff with the self scout, knowing what we've put on tape and how can we can continue to complement that going forward. So, uh, not something that we spend a whole lot of time on, though. >> Over the years as a play caller, have you have you sat down and do the do you do the self scout right away or what's the timeline kind of there? Uh yeah, early in the week we we tend to look at what we think the opponent might be practicing, but uh you know, once again, I mean, there's a million plays out there and so it's it's just not something that we're really we're really concerned about. Um you know, defenses, they are smart and so I think over the course of a game, you just got to be mindful of what they're going to the sideline and they're looking at and what they're coaching up. Um, but for the most part, you know, we we've got plenty of bullets in the chamber and when we when we uh fire one away, we we tend not to call it again. So, I think we do a pretty good job there. >> Last week, Tyreek Stevenson talked about that for the first time in his career, he's going to seek input from offensive coaches just about what they see from him. How much communication is there, would you say, between offensive and defensive coaches to help each other out with what they see on the field? >> Yeah, there's a degree of that. Um, you know, I certainly personally have been enlightened by sitting in with more defensive meetings this offseason than I have in my past. Um, hearing it from all three levels from Dline all the way to the back end. And so I I know it's very useful. Um, we we do have some coaches that have some crossover on both sides of the ball and they they can help fill in the voids, but I'd say for the most part, you know, everyone's got is focused on their job and what they can do a little bit better and and so uh we don't we don't go down that road too far. >> And with the uh priority on ball placement for your quarterbacks, what ways are you using this spring to sort of heighten the emphasis on that, whether it's drill work and then and then how specifically do you grade it? Well, yeah, there's dialogue every single uh day when it comes to that. Um, >> within the quarterback meeting room and we watch it as a staff certainly uh my individual meetings with Caleb. Um, you know, I think it can be as simple as just having a grading system, AB, B, C, D, F, and figuring out where that ball location lies. Uh certainly you grade yourself a little bit harder with those throws within 10 yards than you do the chunk or deep deep balls necessarily, but uh it's something that he's taken to heart. I think he's he's critical of himself. Um and it's something that you want to see in individual drill work carry over to routes on air on over to the team settings as well. So um you know, you far from a finished product. It's always a challenge for us. Uh it doesn't matter if you're a rookie year or you're going into year 10. Uh I I think it's a it's always a big piece of the quarterback equation. >> Co last year was coming off the injury going into his rookie season then adapting on the fly. I mean, uh missing last last year was a big deal. Obviously, it took us a little bit to to get going with him, but um this offseason it's been full till. I love what he brings to the table. He's one of the most consistent players I've been around and that's saying a lot for a young guy because I think it takes a while before guys can truly understand what it means to be a professional. But he he's in early. He's always in his playbook. He's always taking notes. Um I think he he really thrives with uh being available in the pressure moments. That's the type of guy that he wants to be. Uh a lot of trust with the coaching staff, with the quarterbacks. Um and so I'm really happy with where he's at right now. we've been able to take the route tree to the next level and it's something we're going to continue to develop in training camp as well. >> Then given given those um daily meetings that you have with Caleb, you're obviously building a special relationship with him. Could you give us a peak into what those look like? And then more specifically, how do you know what are the tells that you're seeing in the lens? >> Yeah, I mean there's uh each each meeting is a little bit different. this time of year, we're just reviewing the practice tape and and uh carrying on our our ways from there. But um once again, he he's been very receptive to all the coaching points. There's things that he looks to apply uh the next time we go to practice and and he does a really good job of taking it. Um he's not what I would call a rep guy. I think you can tell him something one time and when he sees it on tape, he carries it on over to whether it's practice or the game. uh that showed up last year and that continues to show up here this spring. So, um the more our minds kind of think the same, I think the better off we are in in the long run. >> Takes the spot of OZ on the roster and Oz was helpful for you last year besides the return element that Khif can add. >> Are there some similarities and then some differences to their games? Yeah, I I don't want to compare those two players, but I do have a history with Khalif and um you know, you wouldn't know looking at him right now that he's 31 going on 32. He he has got this vertical push to his game where he comes raging off the football and if you're a DB, you can't help but back up. And that carries over with all the routes that he runs. I think it's been really good for our young route runners to see because it's it's really what we want to see across the board. And so he's been exactly what we hoped for when he came into the building and and it's as good as I've seen him in the spring based on my time with him over the last 5 years. I mean, this he's got fresh legs. He's hungry. He's highly motivated right now. Um there there's a lot that he can do in the offensive game. He's not a gadget guy, but he's unique in his ability to have enough speed to take it over the top. Um make defenses hurt that way, but also inside the numbers, outside the numbers. He's got elite quickness. You get the ball in his hands. He's excellent run after catch. So, he's very, very versatile and I think he's going to be a huge part of what we do. >> You mentioned that guys are going to earn their spots legitimately in training camp. What is your goal for the next few days in this mandatory mini camp? Like, what what do you need to see? >> It's the same thing we've been doing all off season, which is we're looking to establish our way of going about our business uh in the building and on the grass. Uh we made significant strides there. Uh we continue to get better with our practice habits and and what it looks like pursuit on defense, uh finish on offense, all the fundamentals, the block after catch, uh maximizing our run after catch, um looking to emphasize takeaways and ball security on offense and and it's been a good back and forth. I mean, that's that's the cool thing when you watch it through six practices so far is seeing uh the offense have the upper hand sometimes and the defense get the upper hand some other times, too. So, there's a good back and forth going on right now. That's really healthy. >> Going back to what Patrick was asking you about play calling in the last four or five years, how do you how much or how little do you feel like you've changed as a play caller? >> Uh I I would say fairly significantly. I'd like to think I'm I'm better in situations than I've I've been in the past. Uh you continue to grow and you learn um from your own mistakes or things that that have gone well for you. Um and then you look to tailor it to the guys that that are available. And so, you know, we got different guys this year than than we had last year and and certainly anywhere else I've been. And uh the challenge is making sure that we're all coordinated and on the same page and and putting them all in a spot to succeed. But, uh I I I love the challenge of looking at Luther Burton and how do we get him the ball and maximize what he does best along with Rome, along with Coloulston and Cole. And we have this whole whole uh slew of of weapons that we're looking to maximize. And I think that's the fun part. Um the plays don't matter so much to me. It's it's more so how do we get these guys the ball with a little bit of space to do what they do so well. >> How do you like big picture in that regard? How do you weigh philosophically conviction and doing things that you've always believed in versus the necessity to change at times? >> Yeah. Yeah. I mean, you're always looking to evolve. There's there's trends that go on in this league that uh you try to stay on the forefront of, but football in its essence is still about the fundamentals. And I think those those uh building blocks and those pillars we don't waver from and our guys are probably tired of hearing about it this spring and yet they're still going to hear about it in training camp and throughout the season as well. It's the reason why we're able to do some fun stuff, some creative stuff on offense is because they take those simple fundamentals to the next level and and they can apply them and we we can add a few layers whether it's the ball handling or whether it's a little nuance with the route running. Um, and that's where where it really comes together nicely. >> And with David Clark, with Darnell, Wright, what was significant to you your first year working with him about the the progress he made with what you guys were asking. >> Yeah. Well, I think his his approach and professionalism is what stood out from the start of the springtime a year ago up until this point. He just continues to get better. Um, when you watch us on offense, we're certainly uh a little bit more right-handed than left-handed, and that's that is with him in mind. I mean, I think he's a one of those tackles that's a powerful player and can displace guys off the line of scrimmage. And so, when you have that available, it's such a luxury that you really want to be able to sink into it. And and he's proven, uh, that he can do that. And, um, carry the load, if you will, a lot of times in the running game on on his back. And so, u, very pleased with that. I think Roshar and and Kyle Dean have done a phenomenal job just staying consistent and steady. His discipline continues to get better. Um, just like I said, the professionalism with which he enters the building just continues to get better every single day. >> Given that defensive coordinators now have 19 games and the sample size to look at Caleb to study his tendencies, what does Caleb need to be aware of of trying to stay ahead of that? >> He just needs to worry about executing the play at hand. There's there's really uh there's really no secret sauce in terms of uh being able to defend a guy like that. I think he's he's a unique individual and um we're going to continue to to hone in on our core plays, our breadandbut plays. Uh they might be a little bit different this year than what they've been in the past and when those plays aren't working then that's that's when his his uh exotic self can come to life. >> Awesome. Probably grab some Steve Young tape. Um, yeah, it's I have not, you know, we just we see it all uh as quarterback play, not righties or lefties. >> From a leadership standpoint, ideally, when would you like to have a starting quarterback in in a season? >> Yeah, I mean, obviously getting as you're prepping for the, you know, the last few weeks of the of the training camp and into the preseason, I think you want to have a good idea again that that'll come when it's when it's time to come really. It's uh it's tough to have a competition when both guys aren't competing at the same level right now. So, it's hard and it'll it'll come it'll it'll happen at some point. Uh, you know, Mike's done a great job of getting himself to where he is right now. Uh, really impressive to take seven on seven reps and and go out and compete. That's been great. But, uh, really there is no competition until we can actually evaluate him equally. >> Do you feel like two has had a bit of an advantage there just in terms of of like a head start or something? >> Yeah, I think he's getting more reps. Uh, you know, we split the reps as as evenly as we can. Without Mike taking team reps, it gets a little lopsided towards Tua. So, we try to give Mike a few more seven on seven reps to kind of balance out the rep count. A lot of coaches will say, "I don't decide who starts, they they decide." Is that true at the quarterback position? >> Well, I think it jumps out at you, you know, at some point. You've been coaching long enough when you can see a guy, uh, take a lead in a competition and, you know, that's the natural, you know, uh, flow of things. But, uh, yeah, it'll come down to who's playing the best ball when it's time to go. >> How much what percentage of that is just he's completing this many passes, you know, just >> that's a baby piece of it. That's a little bit piece of it. It's how's he calling the plays in the huddle? Can he get it out of the huddle? can he operate the cans and the kills and the everything that we asked to do operationally? That's as big as piece as anything is getting up and getting the ball snapped in the right play. Um and then the other pieces come with it. You know, this the completion percentage is that he might have 78% completion but he's hitting, you know, 15 checkdowns as opposed to a guy that's pushing it down the field. That's very little piece of it. But it's just the whole the whole picture of can he operate sorry, you know, can he get to the line of scrimmage? Is he getting us in and out of the right plays? Are we act, you know, are we efficient at the line of scrimmage? Those are some of the things you look into. >> What do you think about these playmakers that these guys get to throw to? >> It's exciting. Uh very exciting. I know. I uh was with the Rams last year. So, I watched the Atlanta tape coming in uh last year when when the Falcons beat him and I was really impressed with the skilled guys uh the offensive line, very physical, active up front. I was really excited to have a chance to come and work with these guys. >> You singled Drake out earlier when I asked you about Jack. Why is that? I mean, Drake obviously he just signed his deal, but he is such a big piece of what you guys are doing. >> Yeah. No, there's no question. I mean to have him back and signed up and extended that's huge huge for the team. Um you know to have Kyle out there and Bejon and those guys just running around there some serious playmakers out there. Uh tight end group's been really solid too. So it's it's fun to watch these guys starting to come together and form this offense. >> Going back to the the competition of it all. How do you as a coach compartmentalize the fact that they are they're running the same race. They're in different lanes but they can in Mike's case can only do so much. Like how do you separate that in your own? >> It's it's it's hard. Um, but it's it's the way we have to do it. You know, it's we have to understand that, you know, Mike's knee is not 100% right now, and maybe at the top of his drop, he may not be able to put that thing in the ground and throw the ball like he might in two more months from now. So, um, you know, just taking that all in consideration. >> And you've said the word footwork, I think, 30 times since we've been standing here. This may seem like a a silly question, but what are you looking for and what are you trying to implement in regards to that right now? Yeah, we have a certain route trees that we have and then we'll we'll tie certain footwork in with those exact routes. Um so making sure those guys are in rhythm and in time in the passing game the ball's coming out. So we have really four four different drops from the gun. Um you know it matches different routes and different depths. Um just staying on top of those guys cuz we have a big sign in our room that says trust your feet and if your feet are right then you're you're going to make good decisions. And when you get in trouble is when you don't trust your feet, you hang too long and you're off and then you throw bad balls or interceptions. So footwork's a huge part of us. It's a it's a West Coast philosophy that I that I was brought up in. I think Kevin the same with with Kubak. So it's uh it's ingrained in our room and that's how we teach. >> How many drop backs do you have from under center? How many different >> Oh yeah. That we have really three different dropbacks, not including play action. Okay. You know, so we'll do it all. And that's uh that's another big thing we worked on this this year of getting Mike into a back under center. You know, because this this system we we obviously love to run the ball from under center. When we can do that with those guys, it just opens up everything else in the play action world. >> I was going to ask if Mike has kind of more work to do on that front just considering that his lack of experience taking that under. >> Uh yeah, I I think so. He's getting a good feel for it. We work the drills daily so I can get to, you know, put him through some drill work from dropping from under center, which is what he needs after not, you know, not doing it much last year. Um but I think it's only going to help our offense be better when we get our quarterbacks under. >> You mentioned Aaron and Matthew. Those are two guys who can touch any part of the field on any play. How much of an advantage is that for a quarterback when he has that threat on every drop? >> Oh, I mean you you got to defend the whole field at that point. Those guys that can really stretch the field and throw the out routes and and do all the things and make him defend the whole field is is is big. >> Mike Mike would seem to have definitely >> maybe not an advantage, but maybe in that regard. >> No, he definitely he definitely has a strong arm. He can he can reach all the spots on the field for sure. uh when you're talking about the the teaching of the footwork and everything and you're talking about like being on the same page with your receivers, kind of what's their role in in that as you're teaching footwork and like like what do they need to be doing simultaneously down the field in order to make sure that everything's aligning where you are? >> Yes. Yeah, definitely. I think you got to be at the right spot at the right time and that's critical for the receivers and if our feet match that up, we should get the ball out on time and in rhythm as well. So them being in the right place at times, you know, you could have a receiver that runs uh, you know, a speed out that's one rotation too deep and the ball's going to look like it was a bad throw, but the feet were right. He threw to the right spot. So the the receivers's got to be in the right spots as well. >> If Matt Ryan could sort of bymosis take one thing out of himself and put it in your guys, what would it be? What quality? >> What quality? Man, toughness would be one for sure. U, just knowledge of the game, you know, he saw it so well um, you know, as he got older in his career. just the game knowledge is invaluable. You know, I think >> he said I can remember said one time he said talking about quarterbacks and receivers getting on the same page. He said we don't need to be on the same page. You you need to be on my page. >> Yeah, that's fair. >> Do you do you want your quarterbacks to be that way? And are they that way temperamentally? >> Well, I think it's our page. We all need to be on our page and it's the same page in that regard. Yeah. You know, um can't go too deep on a route, can't go too short on a route. You know, I think that that's what he's probably referring to. you know, these are definite depths and and you know, where these guys are supposed to be at a certain time. And I think that's probably what he's referring to.

title: Jesse Minter, Calais Campbell, Roquan Smith Media Availability | Baltimore Ravens
text: coach here with Gus Bradley. >> I mean, not a lot of first year head coaches come into a situation where there's Super Bowl aspirations. How do you think he's kind of handled that basically the pressure of of a new job like this? >> Yeah, very excited to have coach Mel here. Um and all it is is opportunity. Brings more opportunity and I know he's very excited about it. So are we and I think it's a great opportunity for all of us to show who we are. >> Paul he said that he had really big shoes to fill since Gus Bradley left. What is the conversation been like between the two of you as he's installing his system and you're learning the new defense? >> Yeah, I'm very excited about it. I think his track record speaks for itself. Uh it's been proven wherever he's been whether that's the college ranks or the league ranks and I think that speaks for itself through the actions. And so I'm very excited. Uh very clear uh precise on what he wants. So I'm excited to just go out and show exactly what myself as well as the defense are all capable of doing uh within the framework of the scheme. >> Paul, what what about his defense excites you specifically? >> Uh yeah, I just think it's a method behind the madness. Uh and I think there's like uh clear clean communication on uh what's expected in each and every thing and uh that's always allows uh each and every player uh to play uh to the best of their abilities and fast as well where you're not uh hesitating or anything like that. So uh I'm excited about it and I think it's going to be good for all of us. >> Paul, looking back how would you assess your season last year? >> Uh I think personally my season uh it wasn't the season that I wanted to have regardless of the circumstances because you can't control circumstances regardless of what circumstances you're put in. So you control your response and so no excuses at all. But uh it wasn't the season of my standard nor was it to uh from a defensive perspective as well. So, I feel like you got to first start with yourself prior to going anywhere else. >> How much is that something that you address kind of first day back in the building and meetings looking back at last year versus just really turning the page especially with the new staff? >> Uh I think that that starts with uh the beginning of the off-season regardless of who's going to be here. Uh I think we're all pros, so you know how to truly assess yourself and uh what you did and what you did not do. So, I think each and every man has to be true to themselves and look themselves in the mirror. And yeah, there's a high standard especially here on the from the defensive perspective as well as from my perspective cuz what five what five all-pros and and not making it something like that like that's just personal. And so, obviously there's a standard and that wasn't quite there nor was it the standard from the defensive perspective. So, but that's all in the past for a reason and all we have is right now and that's all we can focus on. Uh can't dwell on the past because it's in the past for a reason and life you can't rewind nor in the game of football, so you have to think about it with a a forward approach. >> We just heard Calais Campbell Anthony Weaver's favorite coach probably of all time. What's it been like for you working with Anthony Weaver? What do you think he can do for this defense? >> Yeah, I'm very excited to have uh Weave back here. I think first and foremost he's a tremendous man. Uh what he stands for, how he vibe, how he rolls, uh how encouraging he is, the teacher that he is. So, I just think it's awesome having him back in the building. And like when you just have great people around it just inspires you even more to do things the right way. So, I think he's a great asset for us and we'll definitely lean on him in uh many ways but one. So, excited to have him here. >> How have you seen Have you seen Trenton Simpson grow as you've worked with him over the years and what are you expecting out of him this season? >> Uh I think no one have more expectations of themselves than Trent uh first and foremost and the way the guy's been working uh this the best I've seen him uh since I've uh been around and like it's the first year he's had the same position coach and like where is like the material and the terminology is like some of the same person teaching it to him. So, I think that plays a big part especially when you're a young player transitioning into a new position because truth be told like well when he first came here that was truly like his first time really playing inside linebacker. But obviously this game don't wait for anyone and he's well aware of that as well. And but I know he's preparing and he has the right mindset. He's not making the mistakes that he's made in the past and even if he do make a mistake which we all do as human beings, he's not making those same mistakes twice. So, I'm very excited for where he's going to go and I think he's going to it's a big year for him a contract year and I think he knows that and it's a contract year for the defense as well. Every year is. So, just got to think about it like that and go from there. But I'm very excited for him. >> What do you think about the the front line of the defense? What do you think about players like Hendrickson and Granderson and What do you think of that group on the front line? >> Yeah, no got some dogs up front. So, like having dogs up front definitely allows you to get everyone around to play better. So, I think once you have certain caliber players like a Khalia's, like a Trey, like a Zion, like a Mike Green, like a T-Rob, like a for whoever is out there, you know, and I just think those guys have a standard for themselves as well as the standard with the defense here. So, I know those guys are very excited. I'm excited to have those guys here. Big Travis, Beeks, everybody. So, like I'm I'm very excited, you know, when you have dogs out there just makes everyone's job a lot easier. So, excited to have those guys and I know they're very excited to be here as well. >> What about your impressions of the first round pick on the guard, Vango Euwanae? I know you've gone and seen him across the line here. What's kind of been some of your impressions of him so far? >> Yeah, and I know he's a a tremendous hard worker. I can tell obviously we're not in pads right now, but I can tell physicality is his thing. Um Uh so, I'm very excited uh to see him in camp when the pads get to popping a little bit more. Uh and he knows the game is very fast at this level, but you know, the Big Ten ball is very fast as well, not the SEC. Uh but uh it's fast as well. So, I know he's excited about the op, and I know those guys on the offensive line with Simpson, Ronnie, uh Roger, all those guys going to bring him along very well, but I think he has all the talent in the world. It's just about stacking those days uh day after day, and I know he'll continue to do that. >> After that um strong start to his rookie season, Teddy obviously hasn't gotten a chance at a first NFL off season. How have you tried to help him through this, and what have you seen from him? >> Yeah, absolutely. I think Teddy uh Teddy's like mature well beyond his years, and I think first and foremost, he knows like just like I mentioned earlier, you don't control circumstances. So, what happened to him, like he can't control that, but what he can control is his response, and how he's going to how he's been preparing, and I've been seeing him rehab, and I've been seeing [snorts] him doing amazing things, and like just his mental approach, and physically, you wouldn't you would never know he had a knee issue or whatever like that when you just look at him. So, I know his head is in the right place, and I know he's very excited to actually get back out there and play ball, but obviously, it's a build to that, and not getting ahead of himself, and I know the AD and the training staff doing a great job with him as well, and I know personally just him as a person, he's very excited when he gets his opportunity, he's going to uh take full advantage of it. >> You guys talk about moving on from last year, but the disappointment of not making the playoffs and all the changes this off season, is there anything that you do take from last year going into this year? >> Uh I think you you definitely take things, but you can't carry those things. So, you definitely understand what happened, and what what wasn't to the standard. So, but you can't like bring all of last year woes, oh, how things were run here last year, oh how things were in the building, how questions asked like how the defense was run. You can't take that because like life is not for the past in my opinion. Yeah, there's things that were good things and there was bad things and like okay, you learn from the bad things but you're not taking those things over into the next year because if that's the case then you truly wouldn't be growing. Like you grow after you build off the bad things. So, it is what it is and I think it's in the past for a reason but we're all excited for this new opportunity and like and I like I said earlier, opportunity breeds more opportunity. So, the opportunity to get out and do what we do and just showcase who we are but those are just words. So, at the end of the day it's about going out and showing it with our actions and not just being like a sounding board. >> Roc, I know you want to >> I heard both you and Calais talk about Dante in glowing fashion. I mean, do you think he might be close to playing? >> Uh that's not that's not up for me. Like if he's out there, all I all I control, circumstances are not what I control. All I control is who's out there including my self when I'm out there and all I control is my approach, who I am, what I do and everybody's out there and they're responsible how things happen, not who's in the game. >> Last one, Josh. >> Roc, I know you want to put last year to bed but last week you know, Lamar revealed you know, when was the exact game and moment when he kind of tweaked his his hamstring and you know, how much that injury affected him. Was there anything lingering with you to give you an opportunity to to speak on that and any injury-wise as it pertains to last year? >> Uh like I said, I don't I don't let circumstances define who and how I roll. All I'm in control of is my response. So, if I'm out there, I have to get the job done regardless of the circumstances. So, you'll never see me say something about, you know, to each his own but personally, I don't control circumstances. I just control my response. So, it's in the past, worked on those things. So, it's about just being better and stronger this upcoming year. >> All right, thank you, Roc. >> Thank you, Roc.

Uh, a little over seven months from a a really major knee injury. That would be incredible. So, anyway, I asked Jesse also along with is that full go or you just expect him to have, you know, kind of be doing some stuff on the field. He said full go. And on Tuesday, I'm rehabbing and I bent down to pick up like a kettle bell and I just like back locks up. And it's something like that, you know? So it's not like I'm playing football and it happens. It's like I'm sneezing at a restaurant and my back locked up. >> Sneezing can be terrifying when your back is not. So I'm going through these things and then at this point it's like I can't even go in the car like cuz the car ride just like jolts you around and stuff and so I'm getting in the pool. The pool really was the only thing that helped me. So there was days where I was like Wednesday, Thursday, Friday I'm in the pool or I'm standing in meetings. I'd have a little standing desk in the back um that I'm getting through. So I'm trying to take notes. I'm trying to pay attention during the walkthroughs. Um but I can't even get on the practice field. And I think having the relationship I did with AB and and coach Stfansky when he was here, um they knew like if it was game day and I could move a little bit, I was going to play. And so I think they had faith in me, especially after the first couple times the back went out. Um and so those were the toughest moments because you lose all the core, all the mobility and stuff and you're out there like I'm like I'm so stiff right now. Like I can't move. Like you're out there performing. But in my mindset until they told me I couldn't play, I was going to try and find a way to get out there. >> Yeah. Anybody who's listening who's had a back like backs suck. It affects everything. and sitting is hard, standing is hard. It doesn't it doesn't even matter. Then to go out there and try and play against guys who are maybe feeling a lot better than you and younger and more it's it it's it's awesome. I just want to say, you know, for me getting to know you, as I said at the beginning, has just been it it's been awesome. And you are, you know, in my mind like a Mount Rushmore guy that I've gotten to to meet in in my career here. And you are everything that I think anybody who roots for this team would want in a representative on the field and off the field. And it's awesome. I I remember like we do the Halloween costume for the for the kids. There aren't many people at your level who go to that and you do every did every single year and I always respect that. So you're just to me Jimmy said it I thought perfectly. You're an example perfect example for everything we want Clean Brown to be. So thank you so much man for all of it and getting to know you and be a part of your career as well while you're here. >> No I appreciate it. I mean, it it just being involved in the community and this team. Um, you want guys that it mean something to and it means something to me. So, so I appreciate all all the kind words and uh you know, being on on the show any chance I can get. >> Appreciate it, man. Thanks, Joel. >> Thanks. All right, we'll be back with more Clean Browns. We're going to go get a some tissues here. Get to Missy. We'll back Browns Daily right after this.

title: Joel Bitonio Press Conference | June 9th, 2026
text: All right. Hello everybody. Thank you for coming today. Um, it's a really special day for the Cleveland Browns and our organization. I'll have to admit, for the organization, Joel, it's a little bittersweet. Um, I think Joel Batonio embodies everything any team, but particularly the Cleveland Browns would value. Um, I would argue very strongly that he's a Hall of Fame player. And when you look at the what he achieved here, it compares very favorably to names like Jim Brown and Joe Thomas and Lou Groa uh in terms of quality of play, um games played, etc. Um we're excited for he and Courtney and their three little ones who are over here all appropriately adorned in 75 jerseys and they'll have their dad back full-time. Their dad is already slimmed down. He said he's not quite as slim as Joe Thomas, but he's headed in that direction. Body feels better, etc. Uh, and we're also delighted at least for a year, Courtney, that and maybe longer that y'all are going to stay in the Cleveland area, and that'll obviously you will always be a Cleveland Brown, but it helps when you live here. So, we're delighted about that. I think we'd be remiss if we didn't comment and just all of us go through what all Joel accomplished in his career. As you all know, he was a second round pick out of Nevada 12 years ago and immediately stepped in and started right next to Joe Thomas between Joe Thomas and Alex Max. So that was a good place to start, Joel. Um, and early on had an injury, a foot injury if I remember. And I remember we were debating whether to extend him or not and could he stay healthy or not. And we obviously decided to extend him and I don't think he ever missed a game again, did you? Um, I'll look at my notes here. 178 career starts in his career. Um, that's up there with Joe Thomas and Jim Brown. Um, Joel made here's the most impressive thing and I think you all all know the difference. Joel made five Pro Bowls. Okay, five I'm sorry, five allpro teams. Okay, five allp pro teams. And that's different than making the Pro Bowl. Okay, when you make the allp pro team and twice he made the first team, that means he was one of the best one or two guards in the whole league. He did that twice. Three other times he made the second team. He made seven consecutive Pro Bowl teams. Okay, seven consecutive Pro Bowl teams. The only people to do that in our organization are the names I mentioned earlier, Jim Brown, Joe Thomas, and Luke Rosa. Okay, he was a model of consistency. I I hardly ever remember Joel having a bad game. Um he did what I think you ask everybody to do in any organization and that is come to work, work hard, do your job, be a good team player, go home, spend time with your family, and come back and do it again. And he did that for 12 years. And you know, when players aren't in the building, there's a little bit of a tendency to forget about him. And when he and Courtney and the three kids got out of the car today, I thought, "Dang, I miss that guy." because Joel was so reliable, showed up so often, uh, etc. So Joel is going to come up and make a few remarks, but I just want to emphasize I hope we can find more players in the future who are as good a players and as good a people as Joel Batonio because he embodies everything we want a Cleveland Brown to do. So with that, we'll introduce uh Joel Batonio, number 75, from the University of Nevada. So come on up here, big guy. >> Got a good haircut, I see. >> Yeah. >> Well, I uh first off, I just appreciate everybody being here. Um I know it's a little short notice for some people. Um surprisingly, this has been in the works for, you know, a little while getting everybody's schedule on page and stuff like that. We uh you know it took us a little while but I appreciate the kind words Mr. Hasslam um D you know everything you guys have done for me and my family um you know it is like family here and and I appreciate that. So I I prepared something so I'm going to um you know try and read it and and try and stay focused. It's just a emotional time because it's what I've done you know my my whole adult life is has been here and been to Cleveland Brown. So, um, it's it's a big moment, but I'm going to I'm going to read some of these words to you guys, and, uh, you know, I appreciate you guys being here. When I reflect on my time as a Cleveland Brown, I'm so grateful. I've learned so much. After I was drafted, I had the unique experience of playing left guard in between 10 time Pro Bowl left tackle Joe Thomas and seventime Pro Bowl center Alex Mack. Um, what a way to learn how to be a pro in the NFL. I saw firsthand their toughness, their ability to play through injuries, the importance of being there for your teammates. I took that with me and did my best to instill that in my teammates. Later in my career, I sat next to John Greco in meetings. He taught me how to be a pro, take notes the right way, and play guard in the NFL. I was drafted the same year as Johnny Manzel, and we actually roommed together. I learned some things not to do from him. I got the opportunity to play with and learn from so many guys. I learned how to be eagleless from Nick Chub. I learned to always smile like Christian Kirsy. I learned a chief slam from David and Jooku. I learned how to be fiery and competitive from Baker. I learned selflessness from all my offensive lineman brethren. There are truly too many to name. Um and and the O line is just such a special special group. Um, but you know, just a special shout out to uh Mitch Schwarz, Wyatt Teller, Ethan Posick, Jack Conlin, Kevin Zitler, and the countless others. It was an honor to share the meeting room and the field with you men. I learned how to be detail oriented and always show up on game day for your teammates, even if you didn't practice all week or ever from JC Treader. I got to experience pro balls with guys like Jarvis Landry Landry, Denzel Ward, Amari Cooper, Miles Garrett, JK, and Jerry Judy. I learned the feeling of pride that comes representing this organization among the greats of the NFL. And that's a feeling that never got old. I learned about the people behind the scenes who helped me help get the team ready for Sundays. The people in the building help helped make this place so special. Joe, Pat, Steph, and the training staff who would get me from being barely able to get out of my car on a Monday to ready to play on Sundays. Larry Jackson, his strength staff for the countless hours in the weight room, including Dale Jones for going above and beyond the second half of my career to help extend it. We always have our Friday morning lifts. Brad, Corey, Jimmy, and the equipment staff who always there for with any request. The cafeteria staff who kept us fed. the PR staff, including my guy Murf, who from day one had me ready for any questions the media threw at me. I learned about the Cleveland media, the seriousness of how they approach their jobs. I learned to just answer their questions as honestly as I could because it ultimately helped make the fans more interested. I learned just how hard it is to win in the NFL and how special the locker room is after those wins. Those are the moments I will never forget. I was always remember our Thursday night win against the Jets to open the fridges. I learned about serving the community. As athletes, we have a platform and have the opportunity to make a real difference for people. Giving back was something that my parents instilled in me. Those interactions with Browns give back a kid again. The Cleveland Food Bank meant a lot to the kids and the people who we were able to help, but they also meant a lot to me, too. I encourage everyone to give back. I learned about sacrifice and love from my wife Courtney, my kids Zoe, Benny, and Ada. I love you guys so much. Courtney has been on this journey with me since college and was truly the heartbeat of my career through the injuries, the wins, the losses, always there, always supportive, and always my biggest fan. I learned how to compete and always try to win, even if it was racing to the car for my brother and sister. I learned true strength and love from my mom. Sometimes love is letting you know you shouldn't have fall started in the second quarter. I learned self-belief and hard work from my dad who never got to see me play a snap in college or the NFL but was with me every step of the way. He believed in me and my dreams before I knew what they were. He would tell me, "Why not you?" whenever I brought up how hard it was to make it in college or the NFL. So, if he's listening right now, I just wanted to let him know we made it. I learned how to be appreciative. Thank you to the Hen family, to all my teammates, to the coaches, to Andrew Barry, to anyone who believed in me, to the fans who supported us. Thank you to everyone I was able to learn from. I learned to appreciate everyone who helped me on this amazing journey. I learned what an honor and a privilege it is to wear to be able to wear that orange helmet and what this team means to the fans. I learned how hard it is to say goodbye. I had a good idea back in January that this was the end for me, but this place is so special that it was hard to truly say goodbye. I'm so glad I got to learn and be a Cleveland Brown my entire career. Thank you. Why was it so important for you to stay here to finish your career here even through all the losing and the hard times and the coaches and the quarterbacks? >> Yeah, I was always appreciative of um you know the team drafting you. Uh you know I got I got picked in the second round and and I played here and early in my career they trusted me even though I know I was injury you know Mr. has him, you know, said like there was a question, you know, and and I wanted to always prove him right and and by the time we got things rolling where we made the playoffs and we're having these runs, um I was kind of in, you know, year seven, eight, nine in my career and um and by that point, like you're so committed. You put in so much work here. I was ready to see it through and I was ready to see, you know, the ultimate goal was to to win a Super Bowl and that that was my goal here. Um, but once you once you get through it, like for me, I could never just picture myself in a different uniform. >> Were there overtures made to you from other teams? >> Um, never anything serious. I I I know my agent talked to a bunch of teams, you know, during the combine and everything and people asked if I was interested in and continue to play, like what my plan was. Um, but there never got anything um where I was telling people I I wanted to play for another team. What made you decide to retire now, Joel? >> Um, well, like I said a little bit earlier, the decision was was made like me and Andrew Barry had a conversation before free agent. I think you guys we signed like three interior linemen on the first day of free agency. So, um, that was kind of like me and AB had already discussed that I was, you know, going to retire and I I was I was finishing up my career. It was really just the timing of the announcement. Um, you know, I talked to my agent and and he's like, I mean, technically, you don't have to say anything. Like, you're re retired and he's like, I I've been playing football for 23 years of my life and here for 12 years and you just want to make sure it's done. I never wanted to be the guy that was like, all right, I'm I'm done playing, but now I want to go make another run at it and come back and unretire. Um, and so for me it was just, hey, we want to have a a finite decision, but we were in constant communication with the team and and and they I I appreciate them understanding and uh, you know, I'm sure AB had to answer a few questions where he he knew the answer to, but um, but I appreciate that. >> Joe, you football's been your life. I mean, even the last college, you know, the last 12 years. Have you thought about what the next chapter is? I mean, what the next chapter holds for you? what you you know you want to do. >> Um not exactly. I mean spend some time with the family. Um you know they are ready and eager and and uh be there for them. Enjoy some of the holidays. You know you don't get uh you know you miss Thanksgiving. You know parts of Thanksgiving and Christmas and and those things. I think all that stuff will be very cool. Um but for me on like a professional level I haven't I haven't really dove into you know exactly what I I want to do. When when the the Browns finally made the playoffs on with you playing, there was the CO game and you had to miss the Pittsburgh game. >> You had to sweat that out for them to win to see your first playoff game. What was that game like for you watching it? >> Yeah, it was. Well, thank goodness it was a route. Like the Browns kick some butt. Um, you know, after the first snap, I was just like, "All right, we we you know, we got a chance here." You don't know. I mean, we're missing Denzel. Like, there was a lot of guys that were out. Coach Stfansky. Um, and so but being a fan is is brutal. Um, I was I was definitely sweating and and I was uh it was unbelievable that my neighborhood like knew I was at home and they started lighting off fireworks after the game and they threw like a little parade down the street. So, it was uh it was unbelievable experience cuz you know we got the win. I think it would have been heart-wrenching if you're sitting there and and the team loses. >> Joel, you said in that letter you wrote this morning that you'd never been here before they drafted you, right? you didn't come out and visit. So, why do you think you made such a connection with this community and this fan base and I think as quickly as you did, but then throughout your 12 years? >> Yeah, I you know I am from Southern California but I think if you look at my background in family like it's based off of like bluecollar hard work. Um, and I think at heart like there's some Midwest in there, you know what I mean? and you come to Cleveland and the people here, you know, accept you. And like I said, I got to play next to Joe and Alex and Greck and Schwarz. And um they just showed me what it was like to be a pro. And I I think I wanted to throw myself in it 100%. And I was committed and I was like, hey, I want to be the best version of myself, which is hopefully in turn going to help the team. Um and so that was really kind of my mindset. And then, you know, once you connect with the community and you have all your kids here and you you know, they go to school and you're you're part of it, you know, and so you you're rooting for it, too. And um we'll always be fans, you know, of the Browns and and the community and and the people, our neighbors. Like, it's just a special place for us. >> What do you think you'll miss most about being a Browns player? >> Oh gosh. Um I think it's the people. Like, you know, you you walk in the building and I've been here with like players come and go, right? But they're they're the people in there at the locker room. The celebrations after the wins are there's nothing because you put so much work and you only have 17 opportunities a year and so every time we got a win. I I celebrated full fully because you know I went so long at parts of my career where we weren't winning consistently. Um but it's the people you work with, the training staff, the strength staff, the EQ staff like like the heads of those departments were interns when I got here and now they're you know running the departments. And so I feel like we grew up together and like those are your people that you see on a daily basis and they know the work that goes behind it like like there was times where it was like I'm not walking on Monday and Tuesday and it's like are we going to find a way to play and you know you have to have those people that you connect with um and that help push you through those those moments. >> So you talked you talked so much over your career about just Joe what he's meant to you how he passed things on to you and others who have passed things on to you. I know it's a lot of young, a lot of new on this roster, but as you sort of leave, what's maybe the thing that you hope you left your mark on for the the sort of new generation players that are coming in? >> I think just consistency, like being being who you are each and every day. And it's a business, right? right? Like the NFL is such a business, but I think if you peel it back and you're the best version of yourself and you give everything you can in the moment every day and you have a bunch of guys that want to do that, like it builds up the culture and it builds up the what the team is and who who they want to be. And so if people just see that like, hey, that guy came to work, you know, win or loss, like he was who he is and he put in the work and was ready on Sundays to uh to give his best. to me like I think that's how you build a culture of winning. >> How were you able to maintain such a positive attitude week in week out, year in year out through all the losing? I mean, I remember Joe Thomas saying that it really got to him emotionally, but you just were, you know, you just seemed like you were always there with a smile on your face and you kept the locker room up and the fans up and gave everyone some hope. How did you do that? >> Yeah, losing is not easy. like everybody plays the game to win the game, but I I feel like I woke up in the mornings and I was like, I'm playing in the National Football League, you know, for the Cleveland Browns and I get to go to work and I'm healthy and I'm playing in these games. Um, and so that was special. It was just a moment. It's like what you dream of as a kid and you're living your dream. Um, and like I do think positive vibes are contagious, right? Like if you're a positive person, like hopefully that rubs off on some people. Um, but to me it was like I was living a dream every day that I got to come in this building and uh and be a part of it. And the ultimate goal was to try and, you know, lift a Super Bowl. And that's why I tell people like the best moments were going to those playoffs cuz we were getting closer and and um, you know, you wanted more of those moments, but like those wins and those locker rooms made up for all the uh, tough days you had. Speaking of gohead, >> I want to speak for the group for a second and say we appreciate all the times in the quiet empty locker room that you've stayed and uh answered questions and I think one in particular the walk back to the press box in New Orleans in 24 where like this guy can't ever retire. We need it. But is that something that came natural to you and why was it important for you to always step up and do that? Yeah, I think for me our PR team, Dan, you know, included, PJB, always made it a point like it's like it's your guys' job to obviously tell story about what happened. It's our job to give you guys information to help help write that story, but if we can control the narrative in the sense of, hey, I was out there. I experienced it. I played the game, and if there is something I need to take blame for, I can. You You know what I mean? And I'm not passing blame to anybody else. And it's it's with this Twitter and Instagram world, the longer you take not to answer a question, um the more it it goes. I mean, even just like in this retirement, like there's crazy stories about if I'm going to play somewhere or not, and you know, we just kind of kept it quiet, but um there's just so many moments where I played in the game. I'm a captain of this team. Like, I can talk to the media and I can answer the questions. So, thinking about the last two years in particular, I know you had like some nagging injuries going on, the back in particular that we talk to you about all the time, but you know, through that and the combined eight wins over those two years, um, how important was it for you to play in all those games that you did and is that something you look back on without regret now? >> Yeah, there was never regret in a game I played in. Um, but I wanted to be there. There was a couple times, especially I think this last year where it was close and I was I was uh uncertain, but I was like I'm at a point now like I'm I'm out there. I can move a little bit. And it might have been the wrong mindset for me, but like I was like Joel being out there at 70% or 60% is like good enough for me and I'm I'm going to go out there and try and compete. Um, and so that that that was kind of my mindset and the win loss thing like never had a on my it was always just a personal opinion and I talked to the training staff about it. I was like, we make decisions on Monday if we're going to play or not. And it's not true, but it's just the mindset you have, right? You walk in, they're like, hey, this is what you got going on. And it's like, all right, well, I got to figure out a way to play. And so that's the mindset switches when you walk in the door on Monday. And I just always tried to have that that mindset. Um, but the win losses to me it it was just that's who I am as a person. Like you can't change who you are, you know, winning or losing. And that's kind of just the way I I I stuck through it. >> Jimmy and Andrew and Joe Thomas mentioned you with the Hall of Fame. Like how do you view your candidacy and how important would that be to you? >> I mean, it'd be unbelievable important. It's like the pinnacle of like the individual achievement of a a football player. Um, I never had a goal to be like a gold jacket guy. I just wanted to go out and be the the best I could. Um, it's my like yearly appointment that there's not enough guards and setters in the Hall of Fame. I think if you look at it, there's there's so many elite players and if you look at pro balls and all pros compared to quarterbacks, I know there's difference importance on positions, but receivers, tight ends, like any other position group, if you look at the actual accolades of players, like there needs to be more guards and centers in the Hall of Fame. Um, and so I think that's a barrier just being a guard. Um, but I I think if you want to look at consistency and you want to look at longevity and and um the history of the franchise and some of the names that you know, Mr. Hasslam mentioned today, um, I'm proud of my career and I I I would love, like I said, to be in the Hall of Fame someday, but I don't need it to like any personal thing like that. I'm happy with what I've done and and um I'm proud of that. >> You play with 24 different quarterbacks. That's even more than Joe did. Um, for any particular reason, is there a favorite that you'll remember? >> Oh gosh, in the moments, I mean, it was great. Like my rookie year, having Hoyer back there, like that was a heck of a run when we were, you know, seven and four and I I didn't know any better, but I was just like, "All right, this is the NFL. Like, we're we're flying around. Let's do this." That was great. Obviously, um, you know, Josh Macauen was just like so wise when he was back there. It was fun to play with him. uh Baker obviously changed our trajectory of our franchise there and like led us to the playoffs and that was that was unbelievable. Um and that letter that was you know some of the coolest moments my career is is that season even though it was it was co but making that run um was awesome and then you know you bring in uh Joe Flacco all you hear these stories you play against him a bunch of times and then you meet him as a person you're like all right this guy's a pretty pretty cool guy. Um, and so I mean you take something from everybody you play with, right? But I think those were kind of like just certain points in the career when we're winning the most games and and that's when the uh best memories usually come from so many times about family. You mentioned it a couple times. So I want to just ask you like when you're when you're making your decision, how much of it was it about like it's the right time for you, but also for Courtney and the kids? Yeah, I mean Courtney's so supportive and uh I'm sure she would tell you she wants me at home more, but I guarantee if I was like, "Hey, I wanted to play another season," like she would be 100% supportive of of that decision. But it's great. I I mean, I don't have to tell the kids I can't wrestle because my back's hurting or or something like that. So, we should have some uh some more free time. But, it's it's a part of it. But truthfully, the decision came down to like my body. Am I going to be able to prep the way I wanted to prep to to be able to perform at the level I wanted to perform at? >> What would you have done if you didn't play football? >> Oh gosh. Um I went to school for economics. Um but I don't know. I might have like coached if I had just played in college. I I enjoy the game. Like I I love, you know, football and the scheme and all that stuff. Um but I didn't have a I didn't have a rightaway backup plan. You know, I did some architectural stuff in high school that I really enjoyed. Nevada did not have an architecture program, but um but yeah, I don't know. It would be uh interesting. >> What do you think the next couple months are going to be like knowing you don't have to prepare for a training camp and rigor of the season? >> I think um I was, you know, telling my wife the other day that like it still kind of feels like an offseason right now. Like I I've still been working. I'm obviously not training as much, not at mini camp right now, but I think when training camp starts is going to be the real moment like, okay, I'm retired from this because that's when, you know, se end of July, August, September when everything really cranks up. Um, so we'll see how it feels. I mean, I'm sure there's emotions going in there. I tell you what, like the stress of getting ready for a game and wanted to perform at your best, I I don't know if I'll miss that. Um, you know, even going into year 12, like every night before the game, you're you're stressed about your assignment and and as an offensive lineman, like you're protecting people out there and so you want to play your best and uh and be the best version of yourself. >> Joel, obviously, you know, we'll all share our memories of you or whatever, but just in your own words, how would you like to be remembered? >> Yeah, ju just um I poured myself into it. I was, you know, 100% committed to this this team and and this organization. And I truly always wanted to be the best version of myself. Um to help make the team as good as we could be. And and that that's what I pushed for. And um that's what, you know, I hope people remember this guy was tough. He was going to be out there. He was going to fight for his teammates. And um and was just a consistent guy. >> It's a really tough to try to follow Joe Thomas just in terms of voice of the team, face of the team, spokesperson, uh anchor of the line and all of those things. Did you feel a tremendous amount of responsibility when Joe passed through that torch? And how do you feel like you handled it? >> Um, it was I mean Joe Thomas is obviously like if not one of the best left tackles in in the game. So Andy was a great leader and and a great spokesperson. Um, I think it helped me because I saw him do it at such a high level that I was like, "All right, I I gotta, you know, step into those and I would never, you know, compare myself to what he did." Um, but just just step in and be like, "All right, someone needs to do that for the team and kind of be a part of it." So, it was never a pressure thing, but I did think it helped and kind of showed a way of how if it even if the season doesn't go great, you can still be a professional and, you know, handle handle your job. Joel, when you when you had those injuries early in your career, you know, two straight years ending on IR, did did you ever kind of wonder like what this would be and then did it make it more meaningful kind of to to have that iron man strip? >> Yeah, you know, and I had really never been injured in my career like I never miss any college games or any high school games. So, I was like when I was missing games, I was like this is weird, you know, and I was playing next to Joe Thomas who never missed games. Alex Mack who for a majority of his career had not missed games. And so I was like, man, this is this is weird. In the back of my mind, I always like it's unlucky. Like I got rolled up on twice and I got stepped on. Like that's how my injuries occurred. U but at some point like in the back of your mind you're like, is this part of it? You know, what do I need to do differently? And and um I think once we got on a roll there and it was like seven years without missing a snap, I was like, "All right, I I think there is some luck to this, you know, part of it and and I'm just going to go out there and do a thing." But I definitely was questioning um a little bit of like injury luck and and what was going on. But I think the Browns also having confidence in me and still extending me and and being in that position to be like we want this guy around. Um gave me some confidence as well. >> You mentioned that you your agent field and some calls from other teams and you mentioned your conversations with Andrew and where you kind of made your intentions known. Did you have any conversations with Todd George Warhop and if so how much did they try to sell you on coming back? What was their sort of pitch to you? >> Yeah, I went up uh I went up and met him cuz I was rehabbing my elbow. I had a little elbow clean up. Um, and I was rehabing my elbow.
