title: Minnesota Vikings Players Address Media Following Minicamp Practice | June 9
text: You got more reps in the mini camp. What was the difference first of all between the two? They look the same. >> Yeah, they might feel the same and whatnot. But man, there's so much ball getting getting installed every day. Different techniques, different fundamentals that we're focusing on. And just applying those out here. Yes, sir. >> Can you Can you learn a lot without the pads on? Is there a lot of things you can do? >> Yeah, of course. But you know, you're trying to have the right hands, have the right feet. And you know, once those pads get on, it's going to be a different story for sure. >> Is so much more about footwork? >> Oh, yeah. A lot of footwork. Being intentional with every detail that we're coaching in Indy and applying it to to team periods. Yes, sir. >> And how much easier does it get the longer you do it? >> Oh, my goodness. Not easier cuz this is a taxing job. But yeah, game slows down for sure. No doubt. Yes, sir. >> Thank you. >> When you talk about the game slowing down, especially how B Flow is and how he listens to you guys, that synergy between player and coach, what is that like for you and him right now? >> Yeah, that is it's essential. You know, we we focus on unique relationships, hanging out hanging out outside the field. And you know, really meshing together. Without joy, without the peace of playing together and laughing, having fun, man, this is tough sport. But whenever you're doing all of that together, makes it so much easier to come to work every day. >> And you say it slows down, but in a way your mental part of it speeds up, right? It's more reaction now than thinking. >> Correct. Yes, ma'am. >> Are you enjoying that? >> I love it. I love it so much. Yes, ma'am. Thank you. >> Having fun, playing ball, doing what I love, you know? >> Building off of your kick returning and punt returning last year, is that or kind of a staple again for you or what? >> Definitely, definitely. I want to definitely build off of that and continue to bring what I bring to the table for this team. And also just be involved in the offense this year. Find ways to find different ways to do whatever I can to help. >> What was the biggest thing you took from your performance last year that you can build on? >> It's always room for improvement. It was some some plays that I made and then some plays that I didn't make. So just find ways to build on build off of what I did last year and just be even better this year. >> What stood out to you about Kyler so far? >> Um the vet player he is, um how fast he's picking up the offense and able to tell me, "Hey, I seen something right here with how we communicate." You know, things like that. >> Coach Gattis always speaks so highly of you. What is it like when you work for a guy that's so high energy but sees your potential and then kind of lets you fly with it? >> Definitely, it just makes my job so much easier. I mean, all the coaches, they make my job so easy, you know. I'll just come out here and I'll just play ball.

title: Kyler Murray on Working with Josh McCown & Learning a New Offense and System | Minnesota Vikings
text: Kyler, I saw you talking to Josh Macau. He's from my neck of the woods, East Texas. Having that Texas connection, how is that kind of helping create that chemistry with them? >> Uh, it's been great. It's been great for me, especially because obviously, like you said, being from Texas. Uh, an organic relationship off the rip, you know, when I took my visit. Um, I always knew about him. You know, a couple years ago, I was working out and his he was actually working out with his son in a at a high school nearby. Um, and he, you know, me and him connected then and, you know, I I've talked to him after we played the Vikings. So, he's always been in my ear. So, uh, just being with him now and us having that Texas connection, being able to, you know, shoot, excuse my language, but just just, you know, everything that we talk about is just like it's been organic this whole time. And I think that helps within, uh, the room as well as, you know, on the field when he's coaching me. Kyler, last week I think uh Kevin was talking about he really likes watching not only your physicality but how you're layering the balls, how you're picking up everything. Um when it comes to you being here and kind of drinking through the fire hose and learning everything, where is your comfort level to be able to kind of show your game? >> Yeah, I think um that's a good question. Like you know, for me this is uh you know different different territory obviously having to learn a new offense on the on the fly. Um but at the same time trying to be efficient, trying to be accurate. um and find my way within the offense and understanding uh what he wants us to accomplish within each concept play and all the things like that. Um but at the same time giving myself grace uh for you know we're going to make mistakes. You're going to turn the ball over. Obviously you don't want to but uh this is the time this is the learning phase and the time to do those things. Um obviously it not being real right now but at the same time like I said it can be frustrating. you know, you go home frustrated at days where you don't feel like you're you're putting your, you know, your best performance out there, but at the end of the day, I got to remind myself, you know, this is this is my I don't know how many days I've been here, but it hasn't been much. Um, and it is a lot, and that that's part of the process, and I just got to embrace it. >> What's the toughest part as far as going to here offensively? >> I think the toughest part is again, I was there for seven years. cuz I know I had two different um you know offensive systems, but at the same time uh you're getting all those reps, you know, now having to split reps. It's um me already being behind, not getting the amount of reps that you know you would typically want a guy to get, learning an offense. Um that's probably the toughest part, you know, just again going back to the past, being in control of everything, understanding what we were already doing cuz I was comfortable within the system. Now coming to the new system, learning on the fly, trying to play fast, efficient, and and uh let let it loose while learning is, you know, that's the that's the toughest part. Once that's done, are you going to try to get together with guys in July or stuff before camp to work on some of those things here? >> Yeah, I mean, I'm always I'm always grinding, but um you know, obviously, you know, guys go separate ways, but I'm pretty sure, yeah, we we'll get together in the offseason or in the summer. >> Tyler, do you coaches address that part with you about, you know, the fact that this is all new to you? So, do you make mistakes and it is a competition? You know, how that all kind of factors in. >> Yeah. I mean, me personally, I'm not really too worried about the competition side of things, honestly. Um, but to answer your question, yes. Like, I mean, the competitor that I am, I obviously everybody out here, you know, holds themselves to a high standard. And that's the unfortunate part when you're when you do have days where you feel like, you know, uh, I wish I had that back. I wish I had that throwback. Whatever it is, coach is reminding you, um, staying on you about, hey, this is the learning phase. this is um you know you are new to this um you got to give yourself that grace you know and take it with a grain of salt because this is the time we're trying to get better so it's it's it's all a part of the process >> have you gotten better at giving yourself grace throughout your career >> um I'm I'm being a perfectionist is tough especially in sports when you know playing baseball playing football you're going to fail like it is what it is um and we all deal with it uh but I I think yes in a sense yes how you deal with it and how you um you know persevere through times of adversity is is is obviously what I think what makes an athlete who they are cuz we're all going to fail. >> Kyler, what about learning the system have you enjoyed? Like what parts of that process have you enjoyed? >> You know, I think on the other side of being uncomfortable, I think being uncomfortable for me, I've, you know, I've kind of just, um, went, you know, full head of steam and embraced the part of being uncomfortable. Um, you know, like I said, I haven't been in this position much. Uh, but now being in it, you know, why not? Why not make the most of it? Obviously, you know, there's times I'm out there thinking and stuff like that where I wouldn't be thinking usually, but um it's part of the process, like I said, and um this is the time where, you know, we we're all getting better. >> A couple more days. You mentioned potentially getting together for some work. >> Yeah. >> Uh what is what is uh the summer break could look like for you as it relates to, you know, stepping away to recharge and rest versus, you know, putting in work and so on? as it just relates to kind of stepping away to potentially rest versus putting in more work to prepare. >> I'm not uh I don't look at summer as like a you know get away get away from football type of deal. I think honestly I think you know being a a veteran you know I'm not the type of guy to go away and you know chill or do anything like that. I I'll continue to be working. Uh I know the guys will be um you know we're 40 days off or whatever it is. We're ramping up into the season. I think that's kind of where we can again continue to make uh make a change, make a make a difference and um for me keep growing and keep learning the offense. >> Does the complexity of the offense like excite you in some ways? >> Yeah, I mean you got guy you look around the the skill the skill room and then what KO's been able to do in his career. Uh the guys that he's been with. Um plus you know, would I trade for a pick now or would I trade for a pick in 2030 when Justin Jefferson is on the wrong side of 30 and I'm not sure how much more time I have with him and you know, Harrison Smith and Brian O'Neill and all those guys are long gone and all the players we were excited about their contracts have all expired and now guys are expensive. You know, I've got I've got Kyler Murray on an expensive contract rather than the cheap one I have him on right now. Right now is worth more than in a couple years both for like basic economic reasons but also like logical reasons of as time goes on, bad things happen to you. Sure, young players develop too. Some good things happen but everybody gets a year older, everybody's contract shifts into a usually more expensive year. Uh and ever everything gets a little bit harder to figure out and you get one year closer to your yet last year in that job which would come someday by hook or by crook, right? So that's why all of that's why deferring is worth a little bit less. Um but it also in a very like this is going to be a very invisible hand, very like ca- capitalist macroeconomics 101 thing to say but it's worth less because it is worth less because teams pay less. They they just do. They just pay less for a sixth round pick next year is worth less than a sixth round pick next year because teams have a history of trading fewer assets for a next year pick than a this year pick. Jack from St. Paul asks, I have a slight qualm. Uh-oh. With your trading players for draft picks take. For example, on yesterday's squad show you mentioned something along the lines of you get more It's Boringers you get more Moritz Boringers than Danielle Hunters in the third round. Similar deal with the Gronard trade. The thing is you can't just put a flat level of player on a draft pick. It's a probability. To be able to hit on picks you have to have them. Lots of them. That way the that the way that Seahawks built up a great roster is both evaluation and volume. A big reason Kwesi got fired is that he treated picks like you do and he said, "Man, these fourth-rounders are never that good and then they become dispensable." When really the best teams spot stockpile these top 100 picks. Okay, I've got a bunch of things here. Um I'm glad you brought all of this up, but I've got a a few different things. For one, um the the the like Moritz Böhringers and Danielle Hunters thing isn't the best version of the point cuz obviously Danielle Hunter was a third, Böhringer was a sixth, but I think if you want more a more definitive version of that you look at Jonathan Greenard who was a late third-round pick and then you look at every other edge rusher that has been taken in the second and third round for the last like 10 years, Jonathan Greenard is the best one. So, yeah, you can get a Greenard. But that is if you want to think about this probabilistically, which I think is a great way to look at it, right? These guys all represent a range of outcomes, I say that all the time. Jonathan Greenard is at the tail end of that bell curve and it's irresponsible to think of a third-round pick as a Jonathan Greenard. You have to think of him as a median pick and then think about what you're trading for that, which is why I say like I think a Makai Blackmon, an Alexander Mattison, that's your median compensatory third-round kind of pick. And when we talk about comp picks in free agency and stuff, those are the kind of guys we're thinking of, right? Somebody that will play for you, but will maybe be in a rotational role or will maybe get traded away for not that much like with um with Makai Blackmon and then have an impact but a minimal one or like a Alexander Mattison, he'll have an impact but a minimal one, maybe get 1 year as a starter somewhere in his career and be that kind of guy. That's worth something, it's not zero, but it's a way to you know, put together the uh the the impact of something trading somebody like Jonathan Greenard for functionally two Alexander Mattisons, right? Two third-round picks and because it's the Eagles, I anticipate they're not going to be top five, right? They're not going to the Eagles are not going to pick top five in all likelihood. So, I I would I I I I don't want to be absolutist about it, too. I I have kind of observed that I have been favoring the veteran over the draft pick more lately, and maybe that's just a shift in my own mentality as I see third and fourth-round picks become backup guards and stuff, and then I see those picks get traded for like superstar players all the time. And obviously, money has part of it, too, and it's all this big value proposition. Um and so, that's just me observing that every time I like analyze a bunch of these trades, I I find myself more often coming down on the side of the person with the player, which is just an observation about me and maybe what I've started to value more. Um but not necessarily an assertion that like that's always going to be right in all cases or anything like that, right? Um and then the Seahawks I the Seahawks Yahtzee'd. They they have they they stockpiled more picks because of the Russell Wilson trade. They got a big giant haul out of that, and good for Nolan Ticeley for getting that. Uh or or for helping to facilitate that, whatever it was. Uh but I would say Well, I guess I like the 2020 draft is kind of what you're talking about here, the 2020 Vikings draft, where they stockpiled a bunch of picks. They they ended up drafting 15 players, and they get like seven or eight contributors out of that draft. It's actually like a huge buoy to the whole franchise. That 2020 draft was an unbelievable home run. Uh but it wasn't a great hit rate. It was just that you drafted so many times that you were going to hit on some of them, and then you like you also had some Brian Coles and some other some guys that like didn't make the team, right? Uh or or didn't really like have an impact one way or another. Not to mention, you know, one of the first-round picks that year was Jeff Gladney, who didn't have any impact on the franchise really for reasons we can put a pin in we don't need to talk about, but just looking like that already kind of put a damper on the 2020 draft, and yet there was still all this success. So, that's kind of what you're talking about in in in all of that. And and draft picks are not dispensable, for sure. I definitely don't want you to think that that's what I think. Of course, draft picks aren't aren't dispensable. Okay, finish your final. What are you doing? Finish your thesis. Oh my god. Uh the the deal is short man throw over large man must use big arc. Tall man throw over large man need no arc. Uh and and you you're calling that an advantage because a big arc is good. The answer is that a big arc isn't always good because big arc slower and easier to intercept. Uh now, do your thesis. title: Breaking Down Day 1 of New England Patriots Minicamp
text: Welcome everybody. We're here to break down day one of Patriots mini camp. We just got off the field as you can tell. Beautiful day out there, guys. We watched a little football. Does it count as a little football? Little football. Little football. >> Beautiful day. >> Beautiful day. And of course, I think the biggest thing here in mini camp though is of course who was here in attendance and Christian Gonzalez was in attendance. Kan Booty was in attendance. I mean, I I think the most important thing is that he reiterated that he wants to be here. He said, "Of course I want to be here and I want to, you know, continue to play here and obviously it's about the contract." And I don't think he's dodging that. I don't think that the Patriots or Mike Rabel is dodging that either. But he said that he's going to allow his agent to kind of do his job and the team uh with team and that was pretty much it. Most of the answers were just repeats of some form of that's up to my agents and the Patriots. I love the city. This is where I want to be. And I leave that to the agents. He was asked some good questions. I thought Karen Grigi and asked some good follow-ups about >> Deon Witherspoon >> and you know Christian talked about how you know how tight those two guys are. She asked him if it was important to sort of set a bar and he wasn't it wasn't biting at all. So I thought pretty straightforward. Uh he wants to be here and I still kind of expect that to be the case once this all uh you know the dust settles. But as of right now, still wait and see. >> Yeah. No, no team drills for Gonzalez. Did do individual drills that walk through at the end. Uh so not completely holding out or you know holding himself out of practice. I would say >> as holdins go he participated. >> There you go. >> More so than we've seen in the past. >> Can we call it like a soft hold in because like the full Holden is like he's off in his own world someplace else. Matthew Judon sitting on the mats, you know. the side of the practice field. This was like, okay, he was there. He was active, you know, even when he was watching, he was >> I would agree. >> Yeah. >> In Yeah. >> Let's turn the page to Kan Booty, who I thought was pretty active in the practice. I mean, hasn't really been around there. He was involved in good shape. Looked in good shape. Had a couple nice catches during some of the limited team periods, but uh Paul, were you able to get close enough to Kan Booty to uh to hear anything? >> I mean, he kind of just talked about, you know, opportunities. I didn't he I thought maybe one of the early questions it was there was a huge scrum around uh Kahan and he wasn't uh to the point where one of the camera guys actually asked him to if he could please answer into the microphone because he wasn't always doing that. So it was hard to hear everything. I don't think anybody asked him flat out do you want to be traded which >> is a little disappointing. I think that was the question. >> Um so yeah you I put myself there. I didn't ask it either. So, um, we didn't get an answer to that question, but he talked a little bit about doing different things. I think he was asked about the slot. He said he did a little of that last year. Um, but it's I mean, he made it pretty clear he's looking for opportunity. >> Yeah. It looked like he was in great shape. He caught a pass pretty early on in practice. A >> sluggo, a little slant and go on the outside, ran right by Kobe Miner, to have swag in the back of the end zone. Like, it was like vintage Kan Booty. you know, was like, "Okay, this is not a guy that's been sitting on a lounge chair somewhere or whatever and not staying in football shape." So, uh, he called it a personal decision to not be at the voluntary OTAAS. And he also reiterated that he wanted to be here. Uh, but I think he said something along the lines of, you know, every year there's competition in this room and every year of my career, they just they bring in new guys and new top dogs like Diggs last year and AJ Brown this year. and he was like, "It's nothing new. Just going to carve out a role. Going to, you know, do what I can." >> And real quick before we move on to some of the other uh points, you know, in his defense, you know, think about it. It's, you know, it's been Jaylen Pulk. You know, it's been uh, you know, you know, those kinds of guys coming in from one year to the next. He looks at it the same. Now, I understand that we look at and say, "Well, AJ Brown is a little different than Jaylen Pulk." And it is, but he doesn't look at it any differently. he's, you know, give me the opportunity and, you know, then we'll see where it where where it falls. He was asked a couple of times if if they've approached him about giving him more money or changing his contract, he wouldn't wouldn't really bite on any of those comments either. Uh, questions. >> All right. Well, sticking with some of the attendance stuff, just three names that were not there. Uh, Morgan Moses, we saw him leave last week. He was not there. Caleb Blumo took a bunch of snaps at right tackle today with with the top group. Um, Harold Landry not there. Mike Greyel talked about him. veteran, had some surgery in the offseason, doesn't need to be here. And then probably the most interesting point of these three guys is Gabe Ais who, you know, we've been talking about him on Patriots unfiltered a little bit, hasn't been around, was the one guy that, you know, of the draft class we haven't really seen other than that rookie mini camp. He was watching without a helmet. You know, now Mike Rabel said today he had a procedure uh and that his contract is not signed. He was not here. Uh little bit of a disappointment. I mean, I was excited about this guy and you know, I'm sure he'll still get in here eventually as the coach has said. Um, but still not to have him out here from the get-go, especially without Landry out there just leaves you a little bit of thin on that on that edge group. >> Yeah, I hate to play body language doctor, but you just sense a little bit of uncertainty maybe with that and you know what exactly is going on there with Gabe Ais and he's one of two second round picks that haven't been signed across the NFL. So, him and Cashes Howell who was drafted by the Bengals and we'll just leave it at that. So, uh, you know, >> not good company to be in when it comes to signing those two guys in similar position, similar draft range. I think Howell was like 40 or 41 and AIS was 55. So, uh, top half at least close to it of the second round. So, uh, both guys unsigned, but they're the only two they're the only two second round picks that haven't signed a contract uh, across the NFL. So, it definitely is a, you know, this today was the first time we got a couple of questions from M to Mike Rabel about what's going on with AIS and we'll see what ends up happening, but we've talked about it on the show that when you get behind the eightball as a rookie and then you're playing catch-up your entire rookie season. Now, that position, you put your hand in the dirt and you rush the quarterback, right? It's not receiver, it's not quarterback, it's not one of those spots where you there's a lot of mental uh reps that need to be taken, but still when you get behind, uh then sometimes it's hard to catch back up and these are important days. >> Yeah. And the one uh bit of news that Vel did uh share with with AIS Mike that you mentioned is just that he had a procedure. So there is an injury. It's not just the contract situation. And I think Mike may have been trying at the beginning of the press conference to sort of get people off the trail. Like, you know, everybody under contract is out here. Gabe Ais isn't under contract. So, if no one asked him, people might have said, "Well, he's not under contract, so he's not." But there was some follow-ups on that. And Mike did admit that he uh he had some sort of procedure. That's uh and that's what's keeping him off the field. Guys participate in these camps all the time before they're under contract. So, >> it's not great to miss this amount of time, but I agree with Evan. If he can get back for training camp, um he should be able to pick things up quickly as an edge rusher. >> All right. Well, lastly, guys, let's just get to the practice itself. Um, you know, it's another one of those mini camp practices, couple 111 periods. I just, you know, AJ Brown out there amping up some of his activity. We saw some of the just explosiveness off the line. Like, he just looks like a guy who moves really well for his size. And the other piece, it's not maybe that exciting. If you've been a Patriots fan, you've known Hunter Henry. He just continues to be Mr. Consistency. Drake May, that connection on full display to me today. But exciting to see that full offense out there coming together with AJ Brown in the mix. >> Yeah, we saw AJ Brown very first team period. He was matched up with Kindle Vildor on the backside and one-on-one kind of high point back shoulder just moss them. It was like, okay, there's one's here. Got it. Yeah. So, that was uh that was good to see. caught a slant in front of Carlton Davis later on in practice. So, as of right now, it looks like it's a lot of those slants setting up the 50/50 balls down the sideline and they're starting there, which makes a lot of sense with AJ Brown and then hopefully that expands as we go on. There's a couple of reps that he took that he was inside the formation too with Booty and Dobs out there. So, uh, you know, just baby steps, but it was great to see that one catch you were like, "All right, yep, AJ Brown's here." Yeah, I thought overall there was um you know a crispness and a tempo to the passing game. I thought the plays were getting run pretty quickly um very efficiently. Not a lot of incomplete passes today, which is what is supposed to happen in these settings. Um so I you guys mentioned, you know, the big dog obviously Brown, but um you know, just overall ju just looks like in command uh in control of what what's going on out there. Um and and again I thought the efficiency was there which is there's a lot of short stuff today. Um but um when the ball was downfield a couple you know couple of passes that Raandre leaked out on some uh you know what would you call them like deep >> high corner yeah from back field corner route. >> Yeah there was two of them and both of them were run to perfection easy touchdowns. Um, you know, Raandre's shown that ability to get downfield too at times, but overall, like when we talked about earlier in OTAAS that I didn't think everybody was on the same page today, it looked very, very clean. >> Yeah. Working in the red zone, too. I thought some of the wins for the defense were more getting Drake to check the ball down. Yeah. You know, there was a couple times where they're trying to draw up some shots from the high red zone and the defense was able to force some throws into the flats and stuff like that. And you heard the defensive coaches saying, "That's what we want. you know, let's shorten it and, you know, get them into third down and that's when we can get the stops and get off the field. But for the most part, I mean, I'm sure the, you know, the scribes, as we say, they'll have the counting stats of Drake May probably had two incompletions the entire practice. >> Ball didn't hit the ground much. >> So, even when he got to the checkown, he was completing the checkdowns, which is good to see. >> All right. title: New England Patriots Defensive Coaches Address the Media | Patriots Press Conference
text: Rumor has it you recruited Aaron Colvin when you were at West Virginia. >> At Virginia Tech. >> Virginia Tech, yeah. >> All right. >> What did you like with about him back then and what do you like about him now? >> Uh the same things really that I said a couple weeks back that he's mature, he's wise beyond his years. Um he's got a very good disposition to him, even-keeled, um very very intelligent, um well-spoken, and is a student of the game. He's He's the type that when you mention it on Monday, you're going to see either the correction or the suggestion show up on Tuesday, which I think every coach appreciates. >> When one of your players is going through a contract negotiation, is that something that you talk about or how do you approach those things? >> Like with that player? >> Yeah, like with Christian. >> I just try to make sure it's really the first one that I've been a part of, um but I want him to know that it's involving his side and Elliott Braves, our personnel department here, that I'm in support of whatever's the best for the Patriots, whatever's the best for him, and leave it at that. Because it truly is it's not my business, it's not my place, but I communicate with them, so as long as Braves on his side knows I'm willing to do whatever I need to do to help the the cause and Gonzo knows that, then in my mind I step back and let it be happy. >> They they've done a good job. The The guys that have been here have been It's been good for all parties involved. Weather's good, so I'm all good. >> So there's no kind of like school's getting out. So it doesn't kind of feel >> School's in. So yeah. School is in officially, so we'll be we'll be good to go. They've done a great job the whole this whole process, so they'll continue to do that. >> I was asking Mike earlier about the new ideas he asked the staff to kind of bring in. What do you feel like those will hopefully be able to do for your defense this season compared to last? >> Uh I mean, just just continuing to improve and finding the things that we didn't do up to our standard last year and uh just being able to to add tools to the toolbox. You know what I mean? Things that we got to get ahead of, things that we may not have done up to a certain expectation. We just got to make sure we're constantly staying ahead of it trying to solve problems before they happen than more so reacting to them afterwards. >> You got a lot of young talent at defensive tackle. Well, I'm curious, what are the expectations for those second guys as they enter year two? >> Uh I mean, I think it's the same for not even the young guys, the older guys. It's improvement. So, everyone's got to play better than they did last year. You know, I got to coach better and then every guy individually is going to have the place where they started and then just continuing to to uh improve from that point. And that's different for everybody. >> What did you see from Cory during last year? And he seems to have greater expectations for himself this year. Do you see him making a leap as well? >> Uh I think he's going to he's going to get better. You know, I think he's much more confident in what we're going to ask him to do and and how we do things here. Um but you know, last year was last year and I think there the whole room is well aware of that. Whatever happened last year is is unimportant. What matters is what we do while we're here and and everybody continuing to improve. >> I got a last year question for you. Uh Zach, you know, last year was kind of the inner basis building for Portorreal. Obviously, he didn't play full time. The biggest difference you see from what he was doing with the staff last year to this season? >> I mean, it's just continuing uh continuing to use each other. Um I mean, it's it's a big collaboration. You know, we have a immense amount of confidence in each other cuz we we've worked together now for a while in multiple places. So, it's exciting to have the staff back together and just continue to build off to build on from this OTAs, you know, going into the mandatory mini camp and then leading into the training camp. >> You added a couple of edge guys this offseason. They have the flexibility to kick inside. How valuable is that? And also, is that exciting for you as a coach knowing you have guys that can play inside and out and also outside? >> Yeah, I think just versatility is important for for everybody. I mean, we always say the more that you can do, nobody's gifted enough to just do one thing in this league. Everyone's got to got to be able to add value and and find ways to make themselves un-cuttables. So, the more things that you can do at a high level, the better chance you have to stay employed. >> I think a little. You know, I think it's it's always a surreal moment. I think, you know, try to keep perspective every day, wake up, get to go to work in the NFL is a blessing. You know, as a kid who grew up loving football, as a son of a high school football coach, you know, getting to wake up every morning and and coach in the NFL is a dream. So, I think try to keep that, you know, in perspective every day, how lucky we are, you know, getting to have a work here especially in this, you know, for this current position. >> Think of the day that you found out you got the job and you just take us through what that was like. >> Yeah, um it was, you know, shortly after the you know, Super Bowl, just trying to figure out um just trying to figure out, you know, what the role would be going forward. You know, talked to you bunch of guys on the staff. Obviously, then coach Vrabel told me it was the official. And just like exciting, you know, excited with my fiance, my family, you know, her family. I think just just super exciting to kind of again, like I said, you know, you get to wake up, come to work in the NFL, whether you're a defensive assistant or it's inside linebacker coach, whatever it is, you're super grateful and you're you're super excited. So. >> contract situation, there's a lot of things to work through with that. I mean it it it it would hurt anybody, you know, unless you know, you're you know, you're somebody Harold that's played 10, 11, 12 years. There's not much that you that he hasn't seen. Uh you know, it'd be the same thing during the season if God messed you know, a couple days in training camp here and there. It does, but he's he's a smart kid and he's you know, when he gets here, we'll get rolling and and I kind of stay away from whatever's whatever's going on with him right now and all that stuff, but if we're going to be honest, it does a little bit and that's just something as a coach you have to adapt to in this profession. You know, and and you get to learn and you and you don't I'm a big coach in not rushing through things. Like let's get it let's get it right slow. Even individuals, we might be a lot slower than everybody on the field, but just to get it right. And when I look at this period, you know, why would I say I'm excited about everybody in the room, but when you take Ponder, and I was actually thinking about this when we walked out. I was thinking about Ponder and I think about uh you know, Swinton is when they got here, all right, they're going on their second year. So they learned what they did in the first year. So let's see how now they play a little bit faster, you know, when they get out there and they and they're starting to see things more and that to me is is is is really exciting. They kind of see where they're at and you know, they feel comfortable like, "God, it's nice to to know these defenses and and not have that rookie feeling and and all that stuff." And so yeah, I love their their development. And a year in the weight room and their bodies are changing and you know, hopefully they get they continue to get their mindset changed and get some good always think they should always get tougher, but but yeah, it's been fun to see. I love the I'll be honest, I love OTAs mini camps for second year guys, especially if I got a chance to work with them all year. >> What do you see What do you like about Dre'mont Jones? >> Oh, love Dre, man. He was one of the guys kind of like Gabe I spotted early on and and um with him same deal. You know, he's tough. He's physical. He's He's a good kid. I I know some guys that's worked with him and coached with them and and um reminds me a lot of Harold. You know, when I compare some guys, but they're kind of the same personality. He's a student of the game. Love that he can you watch him play. He plays multiple positions. You know, the more you can do in this league the more valuable you're going to be. He's He's stand up. He's got his hand in the ground. But uh and then you guys can't be here at much practices, but man, he's got it going right now. And it's contagious. You know, coaches can only say so much, you know, before before these guys They'll listen to older guys, right? So, when he's doing it right, when Harold's doing it right, and they're practicing the right way, that's what he is. But he must be a ridiculous athlete. Not that there's not a bunch of guys like that. >> Sure. >> But is that something you could see in some of maybe um illustrated by like his feet or whatever, the quickness that he has? >> I think so. I mean, I think the valuable of going, you know, playing inside and outside and outside inside I've had the majority of my guys for the most part in my career be able to do that. Um when you start doing that you start understanding protections and you start understanding leverage more and how to set guys up and you also realize that, you know, the you get closer to the quarterback one. He's going on year seven or eight and so now I look back and how can I make him a little bit better? What can I do with his stance? Or if there's something he does well, I obviously won't change it. But there's things that I can help him out along the way. But having a guy like him is nice because he's he's seen it, he's done it and he knows how to work. He's in this situation for a reason, you know? And so yeah, he's he is a really good guy. >> When it comes to the younger guys, uh Xavier Holmes got a contract out of rookie mini camp. What did you see from him over that weekend that helped him earn that contract and what have you seen from him since? >> Good. Kind of almost talking about like the same guy. Bigger guy again. Uh he's one of the shocking me. You know, those guys that that just get get uh you know, that tryout. You know, it's not a priority free agent. I mean, that's that's a tough deal to do and to make it. But uh um what I saw from him, again, big guy that can move. He's got some athletic ability, more than people think. Running his tail off to the ball. He's in there asking questions, asking good questions. Still come from college, they most of them barely get lined up when they get here and they see all these calls. But I don't know, I get a feeling in my stomach sometimes. Not always right, nobody's ever right. But there's just there's something about him that I like. And there's something about him that he seems tough. Now, we had we're not in pads and you know, other stuff. So this this this is going to change when we get into training camp. But he's he's got something to him and and there's something that that I've just through the years I've seen guys like him that that have a good chance. >> With a couple guys like, you know, Harold sounds like he's not going to be doing much out here and and Gabe obviously missing, does it give you as a coach an opportunity to get a better look at some guys that you might consider depth guys, you know? >> Yeah, what a great opportunity these guys have. You know, make sure that when they walk away from this thing, we remember who they are. And that's that's their goal when they get out here. He's, you know, he's Harold deserves it.
